questions.stem: Which of these equations is NOT linear in x, y and z?
questions.explanation: A linear equation has the form ax + by + cz = d, with each variable to the first power and no products of variables. The term yz is a product, so x + yz = 3 is not linear.

questions.stem: The augmented matrix of the system x + 2y − z = 4, 3x − y + 2z = 1, 2x + z = 5 has rows:
questions.explanation: Each row lists the coefficients of x, y and z in order, then the constant. The third equation has no y term, so its y coefficient is 0. Writing the coefficients down the columns instead gives the transposed rows.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an elementary row operation?
options: adding 2 times one row to another row
questions.explanation: Row operations must be reversible so that the solutions do not change. Multiplying by 0 destroys an equation and cannot be undone; multiplying by any non-zero constant is allowed.

questions.stem: The row operation R₂ → R₂ − 3R₁ is applied to R₁ = [1 2 −1 | 4] and R₂ = [3 −1 2 | 1]. The new R₂ is:
questions.explanation: Subtract 3 × [1 2 −1 | 4] = [3 6 −3 | 12] from R₂: [3 − 3, −1 − 6, 2 + 3 | 1 − 12] = [0 −7 5 | −11]. Forgetting that −(−3) = +3 gives −1 in the third column.

questions.stem: The row operation R₂ → R₂ + 2R₁ is applied to R₁ = [1 3 2 | 5] and R₂ = [−2 1 4 | 0]. The new R₂ is:
questions.explanation: 2R₁ = [2 6 4 | 10], and adding it to R₂ gives [0 7 8 | 10]. The constant column is part of the row and must be changed as well.

questions.stem: Row operations reduce a system to [1 2 1 | 9], [0 1 −1 | 1], [0 0 2 | 6]. The solution (x, y, z) is:
questions.explanation: Back-substitute: 2z = 6 so z = 3; y − z = 1 so y = 4; x + 2y + z = 9 so x = 9 − 8 − 3 = −2.

questions.stem: Row operations reduce a system to [1 −1 2 | 3], [0 1 3 | 5], [0 0 −2 | 4]. The solution (x, y, z) is:
questions.explanation: −2z = 4 gives z = −2; y + 3z = 5 gives y = 11; x − y + 2z = 3 gives x = 3 + 11 + 4 = 18. Taking z = 2 ignores the sign of −2.

questions.stem: The solution of the system x + y + z = 2, x − y + z = 6, 2x + y − z = −3 is:
questions.explanation: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives 2y = −4, so y = −2. Then x + z = 4 and 2x − z = −1, so 3x = 3, x = 1 and z = 3. The triple (3, −2, 1) satisfies the first two equations but not the third.

questions.stem: Which triple (x, y, z) satisfies all three equations x + 2y + z = 8, 2x − y + z = 3 and x + y − z = 0?
questions.explanation: Check each equation: 1 + 4 + 3 = 8, 2 − 2 + 3 = 3 and 1 + 2 − 3 = 0. The triples (3, 2, 1) and (1, 3, 1) satisfy the first equation but fail the second.

questions.stem: A café sold 20 drinks: coffees at $4, teas at $3 and juices at $5, taking $80 in total. It sold twice as many coffees as teas. How many juices were sold?
questions.explanation: With c = 2t: 3t + j = 20 and 8t + 3t + 5j = 80, so 11t + 5j = 80. From j = 20 − 3t, 11t + 100 − 15t = 80, so t = 5, c = 10 and j = 5. The value 10 is the number of coffees.

questions.stem: The parabola y = ax² + bx + c passes through (1, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 6). Solving the resulting system gives:
questions.explanation: The points give a + b + c = 2, 4a + 2b + c = 3 and 9a + 3b + c = 6. Subtracting in pairs: 3a + b = 1 and 5a + b = 3, so a = 1, b = −2 and c = 3. Check: y(3) = 9 − 6 + 3 = 6.

questions.stem: During elimination on a system in x, y and z, one row becomes [0 0 0 | 4]. The system:
options: has the solution x = y = z = 0
questions.explanation: The row says 0x + 0y + 0z = 4, that is 0 = 4, which no values satisfy. The system is inconsistent. A row [0 0 0 | 0] would instead leave a free variable.

questions.stem: Elimination reduces a 3 × 3 system to two non-zero rows and the row [0 0 0 | 0]. If the system is consistent, it has:
options: exactly one solution, found by back-substitution
no solution, because one equation has been lost
exactly two solutions, one for each non-zero row
infinitely many solutions, with one free parameter
questions.explanation: A row of zeros gives 0 = 0, which is always true, so only two equations restrict three unknowns. One variable can take any value, giving a line of solutions. Linear systems never have exactly two solutions.

questions.stem: Elimination gives [1 0 2 | 5], [0 1 −1 | 1], [0 0 0 | 0]. With z = t, the solutions are:
questions.explanation: Row 1 says x + 2z = 5, so x = 5 − 2t, and row 2 says y − z = 1, so y = 1 + t. Moving a term across the equals sign changes its sign; x = 5, y = 1, z = 0 is only the case t = 0.

questions.stem: For the system x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2 and 2x + 3y + 4z = k, which statement is true?
options: there are infinitely many solutions if k = 3, and no solution otherwise
there is a unique solution for every value of k
there are infinitely many solutions if k = 0, and no solution otherwise
there is no solution if k = 3, and a unique solution otherwise
questions.explanation: The third left side is the sum of the first two, so R₃ − R₁ − R₂ gives [0 0 0 | k − 3]. If k = 3 this is 0 = 0 and there is a line of solutions; otherwise it reads 0 = k − 3 ≠ 0, so there is no solution. A unique solution is never possible.

questions.stem: Elimination reduces a system to [1 2 −1 | 3], [0 1 2 | 4], [0 0 k − 2 | k + 1]. The system has no solution when:
questions.explanation: When k = 2 the last row is [0 0 0 | 3], meaning 0 = 3, so there is no solution. For any other k the last row gives z = (k + 1)/(k − 2) and a unique solution; k = −1 just gives z = 0.

questions.stem: For which value of a does the system x + y + z = 2, x + 2y + az = 3, x + 3y + 5z = 4 NOT have a unique solution?
questions.explanation: R₂ − R₁ gives [0 1 a − 1 | 1] and R₃ − R₁ gives [0 2 4 | 2]. Then R₃ − 2R₂ gives [0 0 6 − 2a | 0], so z is undetermined when 6 − 2a = 0, that is a = 3. Then the last row is all zeros and there are infinitely many solutions.

questions.stem: In three dimensions, the set of points satisfying one linear equation ax + by + cz = d (with a, b, c not all zero) is:
questions.explanation: One equation in three unknowns leaves two free choices, so the solutions form a plane with normal vector (a, b, c). Solving a system means finding where the planes meet.

questions.stem: A system of three linear equations in x, y and z has a unique solution. Geometrically, the three planes:
questions.explanation: A unique solution is a single point lying on all three planes. A common line would give infinitely many solutions.

questions.stem: Which arrangement of three distinct planes gives a system with infinitely many solutions?
options: all three planes contain one common line
two planes are parallel and the third cuts both
each pair of planes meets in a line, and the three lines are parallel
the three planes meet at a single point
questions.explanation: Every point of a common line satisfies all three equations, so there are infinitely many solutions. Parallel distinct planes, or three lines of intersection that are parallel, leave no point common to all three planes.

questions.stem: The planes 2x − y + z = 3 and 4x − 2y + 2z = 5:
options: meet in a line, since their equations are different
are parallel and distinct, so they have no point in common
are the same plane, so every point of one lies on the other
questions.explanation: The normals (2, −1, 1) and (4, −2, 2) are parallel, but doubling the first equation gives 4x − 2y + 2z = 6, not 5. So the planes are parallel but do not coincide, and the system has no solution.

questions.stem: The planes x + 2y − z = 3 and −2x − 4y + 2z = −6:
questions.explanation: Multiplying the first equation by −2 gives exactly the second equation, constant included, so they describe the same plane: every solution of one is a solution of the other.

questions.stem: The planes x + y + z = 1 and x − y + z = 3:
options: meet at a single point, because there are two equations
have no common point, because their constants differ
meet in a line, because their normals are not parallel
are parallel, because both have x and z coefficients 1
questions.explanation: The normals (1, 1, 1) and (1, −1, 1) are not multiples of each other, so the planes are not parallel and cross along a line. Two planes can never meet at just one point.

questions.stem: Which point lies on both planes x + y + z = 4 and x − y + 2z = 1?
questions.explanation: (1, 2, 1) gives 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 and 1 − 2 + 2 = 1. The other points all satisfy the first equation but give 3, −1 and 4 in the second, so they lie on the first plane only.

questions.stem: A system of two linear equations in x, y and z can have:
options: no solution or infinitely many solutions, but never exactly one
exactly one solution, if the two planes are not parallel
exactly one solution or no solution
questions.explanation: Two planes are parallel (no solution), the same (a plane of solutions) or cross in a line (a line of solutions). Two planes never meet at a single point, so a third equation is needed for a unique solution.

questions.stem: A system of three equations in x, y and z has no solution, yet no two of its planes are parallel. Geometrically:
options: the three planes meet along one common line
the three planes meet at a single point
two of the planes coincide and the third is parallel to them
each pair of planes meets in a line, and the three lines are parallel
questions.explanation: With no two planes parallel, each pair crosses in a line. For there to be no common point, these three lines must be parallel, forming the sides of a triangular prism. A common line or point would give solutions.

questions.stem: Finding the point where three planes meet amounts to:
options: adding the three equations and solving for one variable
finding the dot product of each pair of normal vectors
solving a system of three linear equations in three unknowns
finding the cross product of the three normal vectors
questions.explanation: A point on all three planes satisfies all three equations at once, so the intersection is the solution set of the 3 × 3 system. Adding the equations gives one new equation but cannot find the three unknowns on its own.

questions.stem: In a system of linear equations in the n unknowns x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ, each equation has the general form:
questions.explanation: Each equation is a sum of constant multiples of the unknowns, each to the first power, equal to a constant. Products or powers of the unknowns make an equation non-linear.

questions.stem: Which row operation turns [2 4 −6 | 8] into [1 2 −3 | 4]?
questions.explanation: Every entry, including the constant, is halved, which is multiplying the row by the non-zero constant 1/2. Subtracting 2 from each entry is not a row operation and would give [0 2 −8 | 6].

questions.stem: The system 2x + 3y = 7, x − y = 1 has augmented matrix [2 3 | 7], [1 −1 | 1]. After R₁ ↔ R₂ and then R₂ → R₂ − 2R₁, the solution is:
questions.explanation: After the swap, R₁ = [1 −1 | 1] and R₂ = [2 3 | 7]. Then R₂ − 2R₁ = [0 5 | 5], so y = 1, and x − y = 1 gives x = 2. Check: 2 × 2 + 3 × 1 = 7.

questions.stem: Solve the system x + y − z = 0, 2x + 3y + z = 10, x − y + 2z = 7 by row operations. The solution (x, y, z) is:
questions.explanation: R₂ − 2R₁ gives [0 1 3 | 10] and R₃ − R₁ gives [0 −2 3 | 7]. Then R₃ + 2R₂ gives [0 0 9 | 27], so z = 3, y = 10 − 9 = 1 and x = −1 + 3 = 2. The triple (1, 2, 3) satisfies the first equation but not the second.

questions.stem: Which augmented matrix in row-echelon form shows a system with a unique solution?
questions.explanation: With a non-zero leading entry in each column, back-substitution gives z = 2 and then single values of y and x. A row [0 0 0 | 6] means no solution, and a zero row, or two rows that are multiples, leaves a free variable.

questions.stem: How many solutions does the system x + y + z = 1, x + y + z = 4, x − y = 0 have?
options: none, because the first two planes are parallel and distinct
one, because there are three equations in three unknowns
infinitely many, because the first two planes are the same
infinitely many, because the third plane cuts the other two
questions.explanation: The first two equations have the same left side but different constants, so they are parallel planes with no common point; R₂ − R₁ gives 0 = 3. Three equations do not guarantee a unique solution.

questions.stem: The system x + y − z = 2, 2x + 2y − 2z = 4, −x − y + z = −2 has:
options: no solution, since the planes are parallel
exactly one solution, since there are three equations
infinitely many solutions, forming a plane
infinitely many solutions, forming a line
questions.explanation: The second equation is 2 times the first and the third is −1 times it, so all three describe the same plane. Every point of that plane is a solution, with two free parameters.

questions.stem: The planes x + y + z = 4 and x − y + z = 2 meet in a line. With z = t, the line is:
questions.explanation: Subtracting the equations gives 2y = 2, so y = 1 for every point, and then x + z = 3, so x = 3 − t. Check with t = 0: (3, 1, 0) lies on both planes.

questions.stem: Elimination gives [1 0 −1 | 2], [0 1 2 | 3], [0 0 0 | 0]. A direction vector of the line of solutions is:
questions.explanation: With z = t: x = 2 + t and y = 3 − 2t, so the solutions are (2, 3, 0) + t(1, −2, 1). The vector (2, 3, 0) is a point on the line, not its direction.

questions.stem: Three numbers add to 12. The first is twice the second, and the third is 2 more than the first. The third number is:
questions.explanation: With x + y + z = 12, x = 2y and z = x + 2 = 2y + 2: 2y + y + 2y + 2 = 12, so y = 2, x = 4 and z = 6. The value 4 is the first number.
